subject: Economics
description: CPI, WPI, core inflation, types & causes

options.option_text: Decrease in the general price level
Sustained rise in the general price level / fall in purchasing power
Increase in unemployment
Rise in bank interest rates

questions.explanation: Inflation — sustained rise in the general price level over time (not a single-item price spike). Measured by CPI, WPI. Deflation = falling prices. Disinflation = slowing inflation (still positive, just less). Stagflation = high inflation + high unemployment.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In India, the RBI targets inflation as measured by:

options.option_text: WPI (Wholesale Price Index)
CPI (Consumer Price Index, Combined)
GDP deflator
PPI (Producer Price Index)

questions.explanation: Since 2016 RBI's Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, the RBI targets CPI-Combined (rural + urban) inflation at 4% ±2%. Earlier, WPI was tracked. CPI-C is published monthly by the MoSPI / NSO.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Match the TYPE of inflation with its DESCRIPTION. A. Demand-pull inflation.  B. Cost-push inflation.  C. Hyperinflation.  D. Stagflation. List-II: 1. Excess demand over supply.  2. Rising input costs push prices up.  3. Extreme (>50% per month) runaway inflation.  4. High inflation + stagnant growth + high unemployment.
questions.explanation: Demand-pull = 'too much money chasing too few goods'. Cost-push = oil shocks, wage hikes pushing prices up. Hyperinflation = Zimbabwe 2008 (billions-%), Weimar Germany 1923, Venezuela 2010s. Stagflation — 1970s USA/UK following oil shocks.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Housing costs only
Food and fuel / energy prices
All goods, services only
Services only

questions.explanation: Core inflation removes volatile food + fuel components to reveal underlying trend. Policymakers watch core inflation because food/fuel swings can obscure the broader direction of price pressures. In India, 'CPI ex food and fuel' ≈ core. highly volatile.

questions.stem: The PHILLIPS CURVE suggests a trade-off between:

options.option_text: GDP and currency
Inflation and unemployment (short-run)
Exports and imports
Interest rate and savings

questions.explanation: Phillips Curve (A. W. Phillips, 1958) — inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment in the short run. Friedman and Phelps later argued this breaks down in the long run (natural rate hypothesis). Stagflation of 1970s famously challenged the curve.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: If prices rise by 8% while nominal wages rise by 3%, the REAL wage:

options.option_text: Rises by 5%
Falls by ~5%
Stays the same
Rises by 11%

questions.explanation: Real wage growth ≈ nominal wage growth − inflation = 3 − 8 = −5%. Worker's purchasing power declines.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The WHOLESALE PRICE INDEX (WPI) in India is maintained by:

options.option_text: RBI
Office of the Economic Adviser, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)
NSO / CSO
Finance Ministry

questions.explanation: WPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce. Base year currently 2011-12. Unlike CPI, WPI excludes services. CPI (urban/rural/combined) is maintained by NSO / MoSPI.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The term 'DISINFLATION' most accurately describes which of the following economic conditions?

options.option_text: A sustained fall in the general price level across the economy
A slowing in the rate of price increase, though prices keep rising
Inflation triggered primarily by excess money supply in circulation
A price rise confined to essential commodities and energy alone

questions.explanation: Disinflation means the inflation rate is falling — prices are still rising but at a slower pace. Option A describes deflation, which is an absolute fall in the price level; this is a different and typically more severe condition. Candidates regularly confuse the two because both imply a 'cooling' of prices, but deflation means negative inflation while disinflation means positive-but-declining inflation.

questions.stem: The base year currently used for computing India's Consumer Price Index (CPI-Combined, Rural + Urban) — the index targeted by the RBI under monetary policy — is:

options.option_text: 2004-05 (the base year used for the old Wholesale Price Index series)
2001 (the base year currently used for the CPI for Industrial Workers)
2012 (the base year for the new CPI-Combined Rural and Urban series)
2011-12 (the base year for the current Wholesale Price Index series)

questions.explanation: MOSPI launched the new CPI-Combined (Rural + Urban) series with 2012 as the base year (2012 = 100); this is the index the RBI uses under its inflation targeting mandate. Option D (2011-12) is the base year for the revised WPI series (updated in 2017), not CPI. Option B (2001) is the base year for CPI-IW (Industrial Workers), a separate series not used for monetary policy.

questions.stem: Which combination of simultaneous economic conditions is the defining hallmark of 'STAGFLATION'?

options.option_text: Rapid economic growth combined with a persistently high inflation rate
High inflation occurring simultaneously with economic stagnation and unemployment
Falling price levels combined with a strong surge in industrial output
Low inflation co-existing with a very high rate of unemployment only

questions.explanation: Stagflation is the simultaneous presence of high inflation, high unemployment, and stagnant (or negative) economic growth — a combination that defies the classical Phillips Curve trade-off. It was first prominently observed during the 1970s global oil crises. Option D (low inflation + high unemployment) describes a plain recession or deflationary gap, not stagflation.

questions.stem: In India's CPI (Rural + Urban Combined) basket — used for the RBI's monetary policy — which expenditure group carries the HIGHEST weight?

options.option_text: Housing, which primarily accounts for urban rental and maintenance costs
Food and Beverages, accounting for over 45% of the total basket weight
Miscellaneous, covering education, health, transport and recreation
Fuel and Light, covering domestic energy and cooking fuel expenditure

questions.explanation: Food and Beverages carries approximately 45.86% weight in the CPI-Combined basket, reflecting the large share of food expenditure in Indian households. Miscellaneous (~28.32%) ranks second and Housing (~10.07%) third. Candidates often confuse this with WPI, where manufactured products dominate. Housing weight in CPI applies only to the urban sub-index, not the combined rural basket.

questions.stem: The GDP Deflator is regarded as a BROADER measure of economy-wide inflation than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) primarily because it:

options.option_text: Covers only the import prices of goods and services entering the country
Encompasses all domestically produced goods including capital investment items
Uses a Laspeyres fixed-weight commodity basket that is revised every quarter
Measures only the retail prices paid by urban and semi-urban consumers only

questions.explanation: The GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 and captures price changes for ALL goods and services produced domestically — consumer goods, capital/investment goods, and government purchases — not a fixed consumer basket. CPI tracks only a predetermined household consumption basket. Option A is wrong because imports are subtracted from GDP (GDP = C + I + G + X − M), so import prices do not enter the GDP Deflator.

questions.stem: According to the FISHER EQUATION, if a country's expected annual inflation rises from 3% to 7% while the real interest rate stays unchanged at 4%, the nominal interest rate should adjust to:

options.option_text: 7% — unchanged, matching the previous nominal rate before inflation shifted
11% — real rate (4%) plus the new expected inflation rate (7%), per Fisher
8% — the real rate (4%) added only to the change in inflation rate (4%)
14% — the old nominal rate (7%) adjusted upward by the inflation rate (7%)

questions.explanation: Fisher Equation: Nominal Rate ≈ Real Rate + Expected Inflation. With real rate = 4% and new expected inflation = 7%, nominal rate = 4% + 7% = 11% (up from original 7% = 4% + 3%). Option C is a classic error: adding only the CHANGE in inflation (4 pp) to the real rate, yielding 8%, instead of using the new LEVEL of inflation. Option D doubles the inflation component, which has no basis in the equation.

questions.stem: Under India's Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework enacted via the Finance Act 2016, the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee is LEGALLY OBLIGATED to send an explanatory report to the Central Government if CPI inflation breaches the tolerance band for how many consecutive quarters?

options.option_text: Two consecutive quarters, requiring an emergency off-cycle MPC convening
Three consecutive quarters above 6% or below 2%, as per the RBI Act
Four consecutive quarters, constituting a structural failure of mandate
One quarter only, triggering an automatic statutory rate revision directive

questions.explanation: Section 45ZN of the RBI Act (inserted by the Finance Act 2016) mandates that if the MPC fails to keep CPI inflation within the tolerance band (4% ± 2%, i.e., 2%–6%) for THREE consecutive quarters, it must submit a report to the Government explaining the reasons and proposed remedial action. Candidates commonly guess 'two quarters', but the statutory threshold is explicitly three. The target band itself (2%–6%) and the three-quarter trigger are both PYQ-high-hit details.
